clue.text: Burial chamber yields (sacred?) feline and a toilet accessory

parts.note: a feline is a cat, here one the ancient Egyptians held sacred
a comb is an item used in one's toilet, the old sense of grooming

explanation.surface: An odd inventory of a tomb: a holy cat and some grooming gear.
explanation.walkthrough: '(sacred?)' is colour for the cat, nodding to Egyptian tombs; 'toilet' is used in its old sense of dressing and grooming, not the lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: A catacomb is an underground cemetery of tunnels and recesses for tombs.

clue.text: Egyptian-based poet to whom history was all Greek

definitions.text: Egyptian-based poet to whom history was all Greek

parts.words: Egyptian-based poet to whom history was all Greek
parts.note: a poet living in Egypt who wrote in Greek about Hellenic history, playing on the idiom of something being all Greek, incomprehensible

explanation.surface: A poet in Egypt who found the past baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All Greek' usually means unintelligible; here it is literal, since the poet's historical themes were Hellenistic.
explanation.definitionFit: Constantine Cavafy was a Greek poet who lived in Alexandria and wrote much on Hellenistic history.

clue.text: At which Betjeman's subaltern, perhaps tactically, did not shine

definitions.text: At which Betjeman's subaltern, perhaps tactically, did not shine

parts.words: At which Betjeman's subaltern, perhaps tactically, did not shine
parts.note: the game at which the young officer in Betjeman's poem is beaten by Miss Joan Hunter Dunn, maybe on purpose

explanation.surface: A poet's young officer, perhaps deliberately, did badly at some activity.
explanation.walkthrough: In John Betjeman's 'A Subaltern's Love Song' the narrator loses to Joan Hunter Dunn on court; a subaltern is a junior army officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is the racket sport at which the poem's speaker is outplayed, which he hardly minds since he is in love.

clue.text: Comedy films' sound made by campanologists

indicators.note: sound says the word for the comedy films is to be said out loud

parts.note: the Carry On films are a long series of British comedy films

explanation.surface: The noise produced by bell-ringers, tied to some comic films.
explanation.walkthrough: The Carry On films are British farces from 1958 onward; said aloud, 'Carry Ons' gives the bell instruments. 'sound' also shades into the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Carillons are sets of tuned bells, played by bell enthusiasts.

clue.text: Sectarian tailor

parts.note: a follower of the seventeenth-century London tailor who co-founded a small Puritan sect

explanation.surface: A dressmaker who belongs to a religious faction.
explanation.walkthrough: Lodowicke Muggleton, a London tailor, founded the sect with John Reeve in 1651; its members bore his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muggletonian was a member of the Puritan sect named after Lodowicke Muggleton, himself a tailor by trade.

clue.text: Computer language of provincial letter writer

explanation.surface: A programming language named for an author of letters from the provinces.
explanation.definitionFit: Pascal is a programming language, and Blaise Pascal wrote the Lettres provinciales, a series of polemical letters.

clue.text: Kavanagh's girl featured in Reade lecture

indicators.note: featured in says the name appears inside the words Reade lecture

explanation.surface: A heroine from one novelist appears in a talk about another, Charles Reade.
explanation.walkthrough: Julia Kavanagh wrote the novel Adele (1858); Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Adele is the title heroine of a novel by the Irish writer Julia Kavanagh.

clue.text: Hero of Howells work discovers pass to French town

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
ville is the French word for town

explanation.surface: A novel's hero finds a mountain route leading to a town in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Colville is the protagonist of William Dean Howells's novel Indian Summer, set in Florence.

clue.text: Blistering material from an inkling?

explanation.surface: A caustic substance that came from someone who only had a vague idea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inklings were the Oxford literary group that included C. S. Lewis, so the second definition reads the gas's name as a follower of Lewis.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewisite is an arsenic-based chemical weapon that raises blisters, and the word also suggests a disciple of C. S. Lewis.

clue.text: Dramatist who distinguished himself at Blenheim

explanation.surface: A playwright who made his name at the famous battle or palace of Blenheim.
explanation.walkthrough: Blenheim suggests Marlborough's battle, but the distinction meant is architectural: Sir John Vanbrugh designed Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire.
explanation.definitionFit: John Vanbrugh wrote Restoration comedies such as The Relapse and was also the architect of Blenheim Palace.

clue.text: American novelist in with a shout?

explanation.surface: An American writer who is in with a chance of winning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In with a shout' is an idiom for having a good chance; here 'shout' is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Saul Bellow was a Nobel-winning American novelist, and to bellow is to roar or yell loudly.

clue.text: Delicious cake followed by disturbed siesta is ancient history

parts.note: an Eccles cake is a currant-filled pastry from Lancashire

indicators.note: disturbed says the letters of siesta are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tasty pastry and then a broken nap, all long past.
explanation.walkthrough: An Eccles cake is a British currant pastry from Lancashire; 'disturbed' is the anagram signal for the nap.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecclesiastes is a book of the Old Testament, a very old scriptural text.

clue.text: Irish playwright can be read in translations

definitions.text: Irish playwright can be read in translations

parts.words: Irish playwright can be read in translations
parts.note: an Irish dramatist whose best-known play is titled Translations, so reading Translations means reading him

explanation.surface: An Irish dramatist whose work is available in other languages.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests foreign editions; the lower-case 'translations' is really the title of Brian Friel's 1980 play.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Friel was a Northern Irish dramatist whose play Translations is set in a Donegal hedge school.

clue.text: Money gets formal clothing back for Roman poet

parts.note: lucre is money, often filthy lucre

indicators.note: back says the word for formal clothing is read from right to left

parts.note: a suit is formal clothing

explanation.surface: A man gets cash and dresses up again in his best clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' is the reversal signal on the clothing, which then follows the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucretius was the Latin author of the philosophical verse work De Rerum Natura.

clue.text: Did Steinbeck find Mexican food uninteresting to describe?

definitions.text: Did Steinbeck find Mexican food uninteresting to describe?

parts.note: a tortilla is a Mexican flatbread
flat means dull or uninteresting

explanation.surface: A question whether Steinbeck thought Mexican cooking too dull to write about.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: Steinbeck did describe it, in a novel named for a Mexican food plus a word for dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Tortilla Flat is John Steinbeck's 1935 novel about paisanos in Monterey, California.

clue.text: US not applicable in books and documentation recording its past

definitions.text: books and documentation recording its past

parts.note: the US is America
NA is the abbreviation for not applicable on forms

explanation.surface: An official note that the United States is irrelevant to a set of historical records.
explanation.definitionFit: Americana are artefacts and writings relating to the history and culture of the United States.

clue.text: Monumental pillars, like boss dismantled

indicators.note: dismantled says the letters of like boss are taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Tall columns, like a stud that has been taken apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismantled' rearranges LIKEBOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Obelisks are tall tapering stone shafts, often raised as monuments.

clue.text: Godwin's investigator

parts.note: the title of William Godwin's 1797 book of essays, which names one who asks questions

explanation.surface: A detective employed by a man named Godwin.
explanation.definitionFit: William Godwin published The Enquirer, essays on education and manners; an enquirer is one who seeks information.

clue.text: Nabokov's work taking ominous turn

parts.note: a bend is a turn in a road or river
sinister means threatening or ominous

explanation.surface: A writer's work takes a darker direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Bend Sinister is Vladimir Nabokov's 1947 novel set in a totalitarian state.

clue.text: Satellite Titaness

explanation.surface: A female giant of myth who orbits something.
explanation.definitionFit: Tethys is a moon of Saturn and, in Greek myth, a Titan goddess of fresh water, wife of Oceanus.

clue.text: "Nothing is certain, only the certain 26" (-)

parts.words: Nothing is certain, only the certain 26
parts.note: a line from a poem about burning autumn leaves, with the cross-referenced light completing it; the solver names the poet

explanation.surface: A quotation about certainty, whose author is asked for.
explanation.walkthrough: The line closes 'The Burning of the Leaves'; the 26 is the light 26 across, a season.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Binyon, also author of 'For the Fallen', wrote these lines in his late poem on autumn bonfires.

clue.text: The State of the Novel, by Frances Hodgson Burnett

explanation.surface: A report on the condition of fiction, credited to the author of The Secret Garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The State of the Novel' looks like a critical essay title; it is really two definitions joined by 'of the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisiana is a US state on the Gulf of Mexico, and also an 1880 novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett.

clue.text: Beaumont and Fletcher's lady was full of it

definitions.text: Beaumont and Fletcher's lady was full of it

parts.words: Beaumont and Fletcher's lady was full of it
parts.note: a Jacobean comedy title describes its heroine as full of a feeling of contempt

explanation.surface: A gossipy remark that a playwright's heroine talked nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full of it' sounds like 'talking rubbish'; it points to the play The Scornful Lady by Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt fills the heroine of The Scornful Lady, so she is literally full of disdain.

clue.text: Some of the price Nigeria paid for rebellious tribe

indicators.note: Some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A remark about the cost a West African nation bore.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'paid for rebellious tribe' as the definition, but 'paid for' belongs to the surface and is link; the tribe is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iceni were the British tribe led by Boudicca in revolt against Roman rule.

clue.text: Victorien dramatist

parts.note: a playwright whose first name is Victorien, which looks like a misspelt Victorian

explanation.surface: A playwright of the nineteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victorien' looks like a typo for Victorian; it is the French first name of the playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Victorien Sardou was a French playwright whose La Tosca became the basis of Puccini's opera.

clue.text: Eminent Victorians' chronicler

parts.note: the biographer who wrote the book Eminent Victorians, rather than any recorder of famous nineteenth-century people

explanation.surface: Someone who recorded the lives of great nineteenth-century figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytton Strachey, a Bloomsbury Group writer, published the biographical essays Eminent Victorians in 1918.

clue.text: Upward leap for Howard factual writer

explanation.surface: A jump up made by a journalist who deals in facts.
explanation.walkthrough: Howard Spring was a newspaper journalist before becoming a novelist; the printed 'hard' seems to be a misreading of his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring is a sudden jump, and Howard Spring was a Welsh journalist and novelist, author of Fame is the Spur.

clue.text: Murderer of Anthony

explanation.surface: Someone who killed a man called Anthony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a killer of Mark Antony; the second definition is a book title by the thriller writer Evelyn Anthony.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a killer of a prominent person, and The Assassin is a 1970 spy thriller by Evelyn Anthony.
